extracted.intended_audience: readers of religious apologetics / Catholic theologians and clergy defending doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for how miracles function as evidence in religious controversy and how to weigh miracles against doctrine, tradition, and schism. Focused on Catholic apologetics about signs, prophecy, and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three marks of religion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church (true religion) is recognized by three marks: perpetuity, a good life, miracles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heretics attack these three marks; to defend religion one must show its perpetuity (continuity/tradition), its holiness (good life), and the miracles associated with it. The text highlights that enemies destroy these marks in different ways and that an absence or denial of these marks is symptomatic of heresy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetuity / continuous tradition as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth may be recognized by what 'has always existed'; the history of the Church is properly the history of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To know what is true, look to what has endured (ancient, continuous practice and belief). The ancient Church's uninterrupted tradition corrects present deviations; perpetuity is an evidential mark distinct from miracles but complementary to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles as decisive test in doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles 'furnish the test' in matters of doubt between competing religions or factions (e.g., Jews vs heathens, Catholics vs heretics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two parties profess to be for God/Christ/Church and dispute, miracles serve as a visible, public test to distinguish truth from error, especially where other signs (like schism) are absent or unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge doctrine by miracles; judge miracles by doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: We must 'judge of doctrine by miracles; we must judge of miracles by doctrine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both directions are true and must be balanced: genuine miracles support doctrine, but miracles cannot be accepted if they are accompanied by clearly false or morally suspicious teaching. When miracles and suspicious doctrine coincide, determine which is the clearer/evident sign; distinguish by times and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude particular miracles that deny God, Christ, or the Church
rubrics_metrics.description: On seeing a miracle, one must assent unless there exist 'striking proofs to the contrary'—specifically if the miracle denies God, Jesus Christ, or the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular miracles should be excluded from belief when they directly oppose fundamental truths (denying God, Christ, or the Church). In other cases, miracles should generally be accepted unless demonstrably inconsistent with these core realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles are not sufficient alone when doctrine contradicts them
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles must not be taken as conclusive if the doctrine accompanying them is inconsistent or 'suspicious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine must be examined alongside miracles; the abuse of 'doctrine must not be judged by miracles' or conversely 'miracles are not enough without doctrine' are both possible. A miracle should confirm doctrine that is not manifestly false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy and fulfilled tradition reduce the need for new miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: Once prophecies are fulfilled and tradition established, new public miracles are less necessary as proof (miracles were necessary while prophecies were being accomplished).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where Scripture prophecies are completed and tradition preserved, those already-accomplished signs constitute a lasting miracle; ongoing miracles are primarily for times of obscurity or crisis (e.g., to rouse faith when love cools).

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles among heretics or schismatics carry less weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church has never approved miracles among heretics; a miracle among schismatics is less to be feared because schism is a clearer sign of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miracles 'among heretics' do not establish their doctrine; when schism is evident, that visible division is a stronger indicator of error than an isolated miracle. Also, miracle-against-miracle arguments favor the first and greatest miracles on the Church's side.

rubrics_metrics.name: God will not permit miracles that lead into error without correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Either God will not permit that a miracle should lead into error, or He will provide a greater miracle to refute false signs (e.g., Antichrist doing false signs will be countered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle answers objections that false miracle-workers could mislead: God prevents net deception by either forbidding such miracles or overruling them with clearer signs. Thus apparent false miracles require scrutiny for attendant corrective signs or prophecies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public, manifest miracles are more trustworthy than hidden signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles that happen openly in public disputes where both sides claim God are decisive; a public miracle cannot be from a secret enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Antichrist or secret adversaries would not be allowed by God to produce public miracles that convincingly mislead, a public, manifest miracle accompanying non-suspicious doctrine is strong evidence for divine sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles prove divine influence over hearts by effect on bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles demonstrate God's power over human hearts by the visible exercise of power over bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where prophetic or scriptural argumentation is not conclusive, visible miracles provide evidence of God's influence on persons (healing, raising the dead) that can move belief in ways intellectual proofs cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persecution as a mark of piety
rubrics_metrics.description: Persecution and being 'beaten about by a storm' is itself a sign of piety and a mark that the Church is sustained by God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alongside perpetuity, holiness, and miracles, persecution endured by the faithful is treated as an additional sign that authentic piety and truth persist despite external opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles should generally induce change when they surpass expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a miracle exceeds the natural expectation of observers (disproportion between faith state and miracle), it ought to induce conversion or change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a miracle 'crowns expectation'—e.g., heals despite remedies failing—it strengthens belief; when miracles merely meet but do not exceed expectations, their persuasive force may be weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: No approved miracle among false doctrine without stronger counter-sign
rubrics_metrics.description: If a miracle appears on the side of error (e.g., heretics), there must be a stronger sign on the side of truth—otherwise men would be led into error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The balance of signs (miracle-against-miracle) and accompanying indications (schism, tradition, doctrine) determine credibility. The first and greatest miracles historically favor the Church, so later contrary signs require superior counter-evidence.
